planting.note: Plant dormant container or bare-root plants in winter to early spring in very acidic, well-drained soil; Chaucer has a relatively low chill requirement of about 350-400 hours, making it a reasonable fit for mild zone 9 winters. Plant alongside Woodard or another mid-season variety for cross-pollination, since it is not self-fruitful.

directions: Amend soil to a strongly acidic pH 4.5-5.0 with pine bark, peat, or sulfur before planting; Chaucer is a rabbiteye blueberry released by the University of Florida in 1985 and named for the English poet, ripening mid-season a bit after Climax and around the same time as Woodard. The bushes are vigorous and distinctly spreading in habit, throwing out wide lateral canes that benefit from an every-other-year thinning of old wood to keep the canopy open and productive. Berries are medium-sized with a somewhat wet picking scar, so they are best suited to home use, farmers-market sales, or u-pick harvest rather than mechanical picking or long-distance shipping, since the moist scar shortens shelf life. Heavy yields and reliable mid-season ripening make Chaucer a solid gap-filler between earlier and later rabbiteye varieties in a Gulf Coast planting; mulch deeply with pine bark and irrigate through fruit swell, as the shallow, fibrous roots dry out quickly in sandy coastal soils.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Blueberry Varieties for Florida
University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Rabbiteye Blueberry Cultivars

common_name: Pink Cloud Muhly Grass (Taller, More Uniform Gulf Muhly Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Pink Cloud is a taller, more uniformly blooming selection of Gulf muhly and benefits from a full growing season to size up before its first autumn display.

directions: Pink Cloud is a selection of Gulf muhly grass chosen for a taller, more upright habit and a denser, more evenly formed flower display than typical seed-grown plants of the species. Fine, wiry green foliage builds a rounded mound through summer, then in late summer into fall sends up wands of tiny pink-red flowers that thicken into a dense, glittering haze rising well above the leaves, often reaching close to four feet in full bloom. The seed-head cloud holds its color and form for weeks and fades gradually to a warm tan that remains attractive through winter, so many gardeners delay cutting it back until just before new spring growth emerges. Like the species, it wants sharp drainage and lean soil, tolerates heat, humidity, and drought once established, and is largely ignored by deer.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

common_name: Rosy Seep Muhly Grass (Compact, Cold-Hardy Muhly Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil, including thin, rocky, or heavy alkaline sites; Rosy is a compact, smaller-statured selection of seep muhly that fills in quickly and tolerates poorer soils than many ornamental grasses.

directions: Rosy is a compact selection of seep muhly, a Texas and Oklahoma native grass, chosen for its smaller, tidier mounded habit compared with other muhly cultivars. Fine, thread-like green leaves form a dense, arching clump that stays well-behaved in smaller garden spaces, and in late summer it sends up airy plumes of pinkish-red flowers that hover above the foliage like a low, rosy mist. It carries good cold tolerance for a muhly grass and shrugs off heat, humidity, and drought once established, while also handling brief periods of wet soil better than many of its relatives. Cut the clump back hard in late winter before new growth begins to keep it looking fresh for the following season.

common_name: Bonner Creek Beautyberry (Merlot-Red Fruited American Beautyberry)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average to moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Bonner Creek is a distinct color selection of native American beautyberry valued for its unusually deep, wine-toned fruit.

directions: Bonner Creek is a newer color selection of native American beautyberry, chosen for berry clusters that ripen to a deep, dark burgundy reminiscent of fine merlot wine rather than the species' typical bright magenta-purple. Small pale-pink to lavender flowers cluster along the stems in early summer, and by late summer the ripening fruit whorls darken through shades of red before settling into their signature wine color, holding well into fall and drawing mockingbirds and other songbirds once fully ripe. It forms the same loose, arching, multi-stemmed shrub as the species, tolerating a range of soils from sand to clay as long as drainage is adequate, and benefits from full sun for the richest fruit color, though it accepts partial shade. As with other beautyberry selections, cut plants back hard in late winter to encourage vigorous new growth, since flowers and fruit are produced on wood from the current season.
sources: LSU AgCenter Southern Gardening (Dr. Gary Bachman)
North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox
